text: So far every example came with an answer attached, a price or a label. Often there is no answer at all, only data: customers described by what they buy, or points scattered on a plane. We may still suspect the data falls into natural groups, and finding those groups without being told what they are is called clustering. The simplest and most widely used method is k means.

The algorithm alternates two easy steps. First, place k centres somewhere, for example on k randomly chosen points. Then assign every point to its nearest centre, which colours the data into k groups. Next, move each centre to the mean of the points assigned to it, the centre of mass of its group. Then assign again, move again, and repeat until nothing changes.

Watch the centres drift. After the first assignment they sit in awkward places, but each move pulls them toward the middle of a group, which changes which points are closest, which pulls them further. Within a few rounds they settle, each one in the heart of a cluster, and the colours stop changing.

There is a reason it always settles. K means is minimising a single quantity, the total squared distance from each point to its own centre, sometimes called the inertia. The assignment step can only lower it, because each point picks its closest centre, and the update step can only lower it, because the mean is exactly the spot that minimises squared distance to a group. A quantity that never rises and cannot fall below zero must eventually stop moving.

Settling is not the same as succeeding, though. The method finds a local minimum, and a poor start, such as two centres placed inside the same cluster, can leave a bad answer that the two steps can never escape. The standard remedy is a smarter start called k means plus plus, which spreads the initial centres apart, combined with several runs from different starts, keeping the one with the lowest inertia.

You also have to choose k yourself. Plotting the inertia against k gives a curve that always falls, since more centres always fit more tightly, but it often bends at an elbow where adding centres stops paying off. And remember what the method assumes: because every point goes to the nearest centre, the boundaries between clusters are straight lines, so k means works best on round, similarly sized groups, and it struggles with long, curved or nested shapes.

Clustering quietly powers the search behind many language model applications. Vector databases often run k means over millions of embeddings, so that a query is compared only with the few clusters nearest to it, and some compress each embedding by storing the indices of nearby centres instead of the full vector.
